svg.title: Where each class of MCP attack crosses the trust boundary
svg.desc: A map of one deployment, read left to right. A user points into a host, drawn in the client-side blue, which holds two parts: the model with its one shared context window, and the permission gate, described as where the human is asked. Two clients, one per connected server, sit at the host's edge, and a dashed vertical trust boundary separates them from the terracotta server side, where a vetted server holding private data and an unvetted server serving web content each reach a backend: a customer database, described as a role rather than a parser, and the public web, described as attacker-writable text. Four numbered discs sit on the map. One is on the model's context, two is on the permission gate, three is on the trust boundary itself, and four is on the server processes. The same four numbers head four panels below. Panels one and two, into the model context and the approval surface, carry a red tag reading not in the specification and list tool poisoning, line jumping at tools/list, cross-server shadowing, ANSI-hidden instructions, an approval that fires too late, a ninety-three percent prompt approval rate, annotations read as policy, and composition into the lethal trifecta. Panels three and four, credentials and discovery and the server process, carry a green tag reading in Security Best Practices and list the confused deputy, token passthrough, server-side request forgery through poisoned metadata, authorization URL validation, local server compromise, stdio proxy sandboxing, path traversal across two CVEs, and the supply chain of the binary. The split is the figure's point: the two uncovered zones are the two inside the host. A closing line says zones one and two have no normative mitigation anywhere in the protocol and that every working defense for them is third-party.
svg.text: Where each class of attack crosses the trust boundary
The markers repeat as the four panels below. Only the right-hand two are in the specification.
Zones 1 and 2 have no normative mitigation anywhere in the protocol. Every working defense for them is third-party.
